Home/Blog/Electric Gates Stop Halfway or Keep Reversing: What Needs Checking?
Maintenance

Electric Gates Stop Halfway or Keep Reversing: What Needs Checking?

Electric gates that stop halfway or reverse before finishing their travel need a fault assessment. The controller may be reacting to resistance or a protective input, or the installation may have a problem with its movement, controls or position settings. The point where the gate stops is useful evidence, but it does not identify a failed motor on its own.

Stop repeated attempts and report the movement you have already seen. Explain whether the gate stops and stays still, backs away a short distance or returns fully open. Keep people clear of the entrance and do not increase the force or bypass a sensor to make it finish the journey.

Start with the direction and the stopping point

Describe whether the fault occurs while opening, closing or both. “Halfway” might mean halfway across the driveway, just after starting, or shortly before the leaves meet. Use a visible reference you already know, such as the edge of a paving slab, rather than entering the movement area to measure the stopping point.

Separate what happens next from the first stop. A gate that pauses and continues, one that backs off and remains still, and one that returns to its fully open position give the engineer different starting information. Mention whether you pressed the button again before it moved. That second command can make the original sequence harder to interpret.

If you have paired swing gates, say whether both leaves behave alike. Identify the affected side from a fixed viewpoint, such as looking into the drive from the road. For gates that never attempt to close, the investigation starts with a different symptom; this article concentrates on movement that begins and then stops or changes direction.

A reversal can be a protective response

A reversal does not automatically mean that the controller has lost its settings. For example, the CAME ZL19N manual describes reopening during closing when a relevant safety input operates, as well as a response to detected motor overload. These are examples from a particular controller, not a diagnosis of your installation or instructions to alter it.

Ask the engineer what triggered the response on your gates and what evidence supports that finding. “It reversed” describes an outcome. It does not establish whether the entrance contained an obstruction, a device sent an incorrect signal or the gate encountered abnormal resistance. Keep that distinction when discussing a replacement sensor, motor or control board.

Nor does a reversal prove that the whole entrance is safe. A gate can move towards another trapping point when it changes direction. Avoid trying to prove that a sensor works by standing in the opening, putting an object against the leaf or holding the gate back.

Photocells, safety edges and control inputs need separate checks

The Nice MC424L troubleshooting guidance distinguishes photocell intervention, a stop input and obstacle detection associated with increased motor resistance. Its diagnostic indications help a competent person distinguish those events. A code from a different model, or a flashing light without its matching manual, cannot establish the same cause.

From a safe position, report anything visible that has changed around the devices: a damaged housing, a knocked mounting, new planting or items stored near the entrance. Leave electrical covers, alignment adjustments and wiring checks to the contractor. Do not bridge a connection or disable an input because the gate works when a device is excluded.

Ask which device or command was active when the fault occurred, how the contractor checked it and whether the fault lies in the device, its connection or another part of the installation. Our guide to photocells, safety edges and vehicle loops explains their different roles. Replacing one type of device with another requires an assessment of the entrance, not just a matching connector.

Mechanical resistance can vary along the travel

Tell the contractor about scraping, juddering, a changed gap or damage you noticed before the gate stopped. If a sliding gate sticks or scrapes at one part of its route, ask them to inspect that area as well as the drive equipment. Relevant checks may include the track, rollers, guides and the relationship between the gate and its supports.

For sagging swing gates, ask about the hinges, supports and ground clearance through the whole arc. The engineer needs to establish whether the leaf moves as intended before deciding that the motor is too weak. A quotation should explain any proposed hinge, support or running-gear work separately from replacing automation.

Mention recent resurfacing, a new threshold, landscaping or a vehicle impact. Give the date and what changed, even if somebody else carried out the work. For example, “the paving was raised last week and the gate now stops beside the new edging” is useful history. It is still an observation for the contractor to investigate, not proof that the paving is the only cause.

Explain any link with weather or repeated use

Note whether the fault has appeared during gusty weather, after rain or after several movements close together. The HSE identifies weather, debris, wear and the condition of connections as factors in powered-gate safety. The Nice manual also explains that motor-current readings can vary with friction and wind, and distinguishes excessive consecutive movements in its diagnostics.

Those patterns help the engineer plan the visit. They do not justify labelling the fault “water damage” or “an overheating motor” without inspection. If the entrance worked during the last service but failed after a busy morning, give both facts. For a shared driveway, ask residents to pass observations to one person rather than making separate attempts to reproduce the problem.

A fault that disappears before the visit still deserves a clear record. Keep the date, weather and description of the movement. Share an existing fixed-camera clip if it shows the event, with unrelated footage and access information removed. Do not run a suspect gate again just to obtain a video.

Check the intended opening sequence with the installer

A deliberate partial-opening function can look like a gate stopping early if you expect vehicle access. The CAME manual includes partial-opening and stop commands, illustrating why the control used matters. Tell the contractor which button or access method you used and what that same command previously did.

Report whether the problem began after a new remote, a control change, a service visit or manual release. Ask the engineer to check the intended travel and stopping arrangements against the actual installation. Do not start a learning cycle, move limit devices or perform a factory reset before the cause is understood.

If someone else manages the entrance, establish who may authorise changes. Keep the engineer’s explanation of the full-opening and pedestrian functions with the handover records. Residents should not have to guess whether a shortened opening is deliberate or a fault that has been left unresolved.

Do not turn up the force to get past the fault

Increasing force can change how the gate responds to resistance. It may also leave the original mechanical or control problem unresolved. Any adjustment needs to form part of competent assessment and testing, rather than a homeowner experiment to get the entrance moving again.

The HSE’s guidance on powered-gate safety treats the completed installation as a whole. Where force limitation provides the primary protection, objective force testing forms part of checking safety. Ask which checks your repair needs and request the relevant records. Our explanation of electric gate force testing sets out useful questions for the contractor.

Agree safe access while the fault remains unresolved

If the gate moves unpredictably, appears unstable or presents a trapping risk, keep it out of use and seek competent help. Follow the shutdown instructions supplied for your installation only where you can do so safely. Do not push against a powered leaf, enter a gap that could close or improvise a restraint.

Ask the contractor how the entrance can be left secure while awaiting work. Explain if it is the only vehicle route or serves several households. Manual release is specific to the operator and the condition of the gate; releasing a damaged or poorly restrained leaf can introduce another problem. Tell the contractor if you lack the key, instructions or a safe alternative route.

Send a concise fault brief before booking

A clear enquiry helps the repair company decide what information and equipment it needs before attending. You do not need to diagnose the failed part. Describe the symptom, give the postcode and include the make or model from records or a label you can read without removing a cover.

  1. State whether the gate is sliding or swinging, and whether one leaf or the whole entrance is affected.
  2. Describe the direction of travel, where the movement stops and how far it reverses, if at all.
  3. Name the control used and say whether this behaviour is new or part of the usual opening sequence.
  4. Mention recent work, damage, weather or interrupted power, with dates where possible.
  5. Explain the access difficulty and ask about the attendance charge, investigation scope and approval of additional work.

Keep your observations separate from suggestions somebody has made. “The left leaf stops beside the drain” is an observation; “the motor needs replacing” is a proposal that needs evidence. If you have a previous report or quotation, include it so the next contractor can explain what it agrees with and what still needs checking.

Compare the repair scope and check the handover

Ask for the finding, the proposed remedy and the total work included. A repair might involve mechanical work, a protective device, a connection or control equipment, depending on the diagnosis. Ask what will be retained, which settings will change and how the engineer will check the reported fault after the work.

Separate the investigation charge from optional improvements. If a contractor recommends wider replacement, ask why a smaller repair would not address the problem and what compatibility or condition issue limits the choices. There is no reliable fixed repair price for “gates reversing” without knowing the installed system and the cause.

At handover, ask for an explanation of the corrected behaviour, any changed controls and the maintenance instructions relevant to the repair. Keep the findings and test records with your gate documents. When requesting electric gate repair and maintenance, describe the stopping or reversing sequence so the enquiry starts with the fault you need resolved.

Tell us where the movement stops and what happens next, using what you have already observed. Ask about investigating the fault and the repair work your gates may need.

Home/Blog/Electric Gates Not Working After Rain? Water Damage and Repair Options
Maintenance

Electric Gates Not Working After Rain? Water Damage and Repair Options

Electric gates that stop working after rain need an investigation of the installed system, not an automatic motor replacement. Water may have reached electrical equipment, a protective device may be responding, or rain may have coincided with a separate fault. The pattern is useful evidence, but it does not identify the damaged part.

The short takeaway: stop repeated attempts, keep clear of suspect equipment and report what happened. Do not open electrical covers, bypass a sensor or try to dry out the controls yourself. If flooding or electrical damage is suspected, arrange competent help before using the gates again.

Start with the symptom, not a diagnosis of water damage

Describe whether the entrance is completely unresponsive, one leaf stays still, or movement starts and then stops. Say whether the gate opened normally before the rain began and whether the fault appeared during the downpour or later. Those details give the contractor a starting point without assuming that every wet-weather failure has the same cause.

For example, “both leaves opened at seven, but neither responded after the storm” is more useful than “the rain has broken the motor”. Include whether other household equipment also lost power. If you already know that a protective device has operated, report that fact; do not restore the supply repeatedly to see what happens.

Keep the direction of travel clear. A gate that opens but will not close presents a different sequence from one that never moves. If your main symptom is gates opening but refusing to close, describe that alongside the weather. The engineer still needs to establish which input, connection or component is involved.

Treat flooding and damaged electrics as a separate safety concern

Standing water around electrical equipment, a damaged enclosure or exposed cable calls for caution. Keep people away and seek professional advice. Do not walk into water to reach a gate isolator or control box. Follow your installation’s shutdown instructions only if you can do so safely; an uncertain electrical condition is a reason to stop, not improvise.

Electrical Safety First’s advice after flooding says not to touch a wet or damaged fuse box and to have affected electrical equipment assessed by a registered electrician before use. That is flood-safety guidance, rather than a diagnosis of a gate fault. Tell the gate contractor if electrical damage or a supply problem may need an electrician’s involvement.

A return to dry weather does not establish that affected equipment is safe. Do not treat a working remote response the following morning as clearance to resume normal operation after suspected flooding. Explain what was wet, where water was visible and whether anybody has already isolated or inspected the installation.

Ask about connections and enclosures as well as the motor

The HSE’s powered-gate safety guidance identifies weather and water ingress at wiring and connections as factors that can affect safe operation. The completed entrance needs assessment as a system. A motor is only one part of that system, so a quotation based solely on the timing of the rain needs a clearer explanation.

Ask the contractor what it found, how it established the fault and which equipment needs attention. Depending on the finding, the proposed work might concern a connection, cable entry, enclosure, device or drive component. These are possible areas for investigation, not a list of parts that should all be changed.

Keep any previous repair report available. If an enclosure was replaced recently, tell the contractor when and who did it. Ask whether the new proposal addresses the route by which water entered, where ingress is confirmed. Replacing a damaged component without explaining the underlying cause leaves an important question unanswered.

A wet-weather closing fault may involve a protective input

If the gate starts normally but changes behaviour around its safety devices, tell the engineer exactly what you observed. Do not assume that a photocell has failed simply because the problem appeared in rain. A device, its mounting, its connection and the controller’s response need to be distinguished.

Report visible changes from outside the movement area, such as a cracked housing, a knocked post or planting that has grown across the entrance. You do not need to remove a cover or alter alignment to make a useful enquiry. Our guide to photocells, safety edges and vehicle loops explains why these devices have different roles.

Never disable a device to restore access. Nor should you stand in the opening or place an object against a moving leaf to test it. If movement begins and then changes direction, describe the stopping point and use our explanation of gates stopping halfway or reversing for the details worth recording from an event you have already seen.

Check whether the entrance itself changed during the rain

Tell the contractor about leaves, silt, displaced gravel or a new area of standing water visible near the gate. Mention recent paving, landscaping or drainage work, particularly if the first failure followed that work. These observations may help explain what has changed at the entrance; they do not prove an electrical or mechanical cause.

Keep observation separate from intervention. Do not reach into a track, under a leaf or beside drive equipment while the system could move. Ask the contractor what routine cleaning is appropriate for your installation once it has been made safe, and which tasks belong to its maintenance visit.

Photographs taken from a safe position can show the water’s location and the surrounding ground. A wide view is often more useful than a close-up of a closed control box. Do not lift a motor-box lid, disturb wiring or operate the gates again just to obtain a better picture.

Underground motor boxes need a drainage assessment

Where the operators sit below ground, explain whether water was visible around the covers and whether this happens after every shower or only prolonged rain. A wet cover alone does not establish what has happened inside. Leave opening and inspecting the box to the contractor, especially where the gate’s movement or electrical condition is uncertain.

Drainage is part of the installation detail, not a universal afterthought. For example, the CAME FROG-PC foundation-box instructions provide for drainage tubing as well as electrical cable routes. That is a model-specific example; your contractor should use the instructions and site conditions relevant to your own equipment.

If flooded underground motor boxes are suspected, ask for separate findings on the operator, its housing and the drainage arrangement. A replacement motor and a change to drainage are different items of work. Ask what evidence supports each, what remains in place and who is responsible for any groundworks. Do not drill holes or pump water beside electrical equipment yourself.

Compare repairs with replacement on a defined scope

A useful quotation names the fault found and explains the proposed remedy. Ask whether the investigation is included in the attendance charge, what further work needs approval and which existing parts will be retained. There is no dependable fixed price for a rain-related gate fault without knowing the equipment, access and damage involved.

Where water damage is confirmed, ask which components are repairable and which require replacement, with the reason for each decision. Keep that separate from optional improvements. If wider replacement is recommended, ask why a limited repair would not resolve the problem and whether compatibility or the condition of other parts affects the choice.

If you have already paid for several wet-weather repairs, gather the earlier findings rather than comparing only the latest price. Our guide to repairing gates that keep breaking down helps you compare the wider decision. A repeated symptom still needs evidence about its cause; it does not, by itself, prove that the entire gate must be replaced.

Prepare a clear enquiry and agree temporary access

Send the postcode, gate type and make or model from records or a label you can read safely. Explain whether the entrance serves one home or several and whether it is your only vehicle access. If the gate position creates an immediate access problem, say so before the visit rather than attempting an unfamiliar manual release.

  1. Give the date and describe the rain, any visible flooding and when the fault first appeared.
  2. State which leaf or function stopped working and what happened after the last normal command.
  3. Mention any known power interruption, operated protective device or recent work without trying to reproduce it.
  4. Attach existing reports and safe photographs, keeping access codes and unrelated personal details out.
  5. Ask about attendance charges, the investigation scope and how repair costs will be approved.

For gates that trip the electrics, make that symptom explicit when booking. It may change the help needed, particularly if other circuits are affected. Ask the contractor how the entrance can be left safe while awaiting repairs. A released leaf may move differently from a powered one, so do not push, restrain or disconnect it without the installation-specific instructions and safe conditions.

Check the handover and plan for the next wet spell

At handover, ask for the diagnosed cause, the work completed and the checks appropriate to that repair. If ingress was found, the record should explain what was done about it as well as which damaged parts were replaced. Keep any relevant test records and updated operating instructions with the gate documents.

Ask what you should report if the symptom returns and which routine observations will help. Agree maintenance tasks for your particular entrance rather than adding sealant, covering equipment with plastic or changing settings yourself. Where drainage or paving work is outside the gate contractor’s scope, establish who will specify and complete it before considering the whole problem resolved.

When requesting electric gate repair and maintenance, describe the rain-related pattern and your access needs. That gives the enquiry a practical purpose: identifying the fault, understanding the repair options and addressing the relevant installation issue before normal use resumes.

Gates stopped working after rain?

Tell us what stopped working and where you noticed water. Ask about investigating the rain-related fault and the repair work your gates may need.

Home/Blog/Electric Gates Keep Tripping the Electrics: When to Call an Engineer
Maintenance

Electric Gates Keep Tripping the Electrics: When to Call an Engineer

When electric gates keep tripping the electrics, a protective device in your consumer unit is switching off the supply because it has detected a problem. The gate is a sensible place to look, especially if the trip happens when the gate moves, but the timing alone does not prove which part is at fault. Treat a repeated trip as a fault report from the installation, not a nuisance to be worked around.

The short takeaway: reset the tripped device once, and only if it is safe to do so. If it trips again, leave it off and call a qualified electrician or gate engineer. Do not open the control box, motor covers or any junction box, and do not try to find the faulty circuit yourself at the consumer unit.

Tripped RCDs, Breakers and Fuses

A modern consumer unit has a main switch with fuses or circuit breakers, and often one or more residual current devices (RCDs). An RCD switches off when it detects current leaking from a circuit, which can happen when damp or damage lets electricity escape where it should not. A fuse or circuit breaker generally cuts off when too much current flows, through an overload or a fault. Both are doing their job when they operate.

You do not need to interpret which device has operated, but it is useful information for whoever attends. Note whether a single switch has dropped or a whole bank of circuits has gone off, and read the labels without removing any cover. Some installations also have a separate isolator or small consumer unit near the gate. Tell the engineer where you found the switch that was off.

Electrical Safety First’s advice for householders lists circuit breakers tripping among the warning signs that call for a registered electrician to check your electrics as soon as possible. A gate that trips the supply once after a storm and then works normally still deserves a mention when you book its next service.

The Pattern Worth Recording

The moment of the trip narrows the search more than any guess about the motor. Write down what was happening each time, from a safe position and without operating the gate just to repeat the fault. A short note made on the day is more reliable than a recollection a week later.

  • Did the trip happen as soon as the gate received a command, partway through travel, or while it was standing still?
  • Did it coincide with rain, frost or a period of standing water? Trips that cluster around faults following wet weather point the investigation towards water ingress.
  • Did lights, sockets or other outdoor equipment also lose power, or only the gate?
  • Was anything else running at the time, such as garden lighting, a pond pump or an outdoor socket on the same circuit?
  • Has there been recent digging, paving, fencing or planting along the route the gate cable is likely to take?

Keep the dates and times together with any earlier repair reports. If the gate shares a circuit with other outdoor equipment, say so. The electrician may need to separate those loads during testing, and the gate engineer will want to know that a trip might not originate at the gate at all.

Safe Checks Before You Call

Your part is limited to looking and, at most, one reset. Stay away from the consumer unit if it is damaged, hot, wet, scorched or making a crackling sound, and if you can smell burning. In those cases leave everything off and get professional help. Never touch electrical equipment with wet hands or while standing in water.

  1. Look at the consumer unit and identify which switch is off. Do not remove its cover.
  2. If nothing looks or smells wrong, switch that device back on once.
  3. If it trips again straight away or the next time the gate runs, switch nothing else and leave it off.
  4. From a safe distance, look for obvious damage at the gate, such as a cracked housing, a cable pulled loose or water pooling around equipment. Do not touch or open anything.
  5. Call a qualified electrician or your gate engineer and describe what you saw.

Online advice sometimes suggests switching circuits off one by one at the consumer unit, disconnecting wires or trying a different breaker until the trip stops. Work inside the consumer unit or on fixed wiring belongs to an electrician with the right test equipment. Never tape, wedge or hold a protective device on, or ask anyone to bypass it to keep the gate running.

Access While the Gate Is Switched Off

With the gate supply off, remotes, keypads and the intercom may stop working. If you need the entrance open, follow the manual-release instructions for your gate supplied with your particular system. A released leaf can move in the wind or under its own weight, so keep people, pets and vehicles clear and secure it only in the way the instructions describe.

Do not restore power to test whether the gate has recovered. Tell anyone else who uses the entrance, including neighbours on a shared driveway, that the gate is out of use and why. If an engineer is coming, agree whether the gate should be left open or closed before the visit.

Possible Leakage Points on a Gate Installation

The HSE’s powered gate guidance warns that water ingress or damage to cabling, control boxes and the connections between components may result in a risk of electric shock or a failure to operate safely. It also says powered gates should be installed and maintained by competent contractors. A gate installation has several places where moisture or damage can reach live parts, and none of them can be ruled out from the driveway.

Possible areas for investigation include the supply cable between the house and the gate, junction boxes along the route, the control panel, the motors, and accessories such as photocells, keypads, intercom units and lighting. Where operators sit below ground, water around an underground motor is a specific line of enquiry. These are places an engineer may test, not a list of parts that need replacing.

A fault may also come from equipment that shares the gate circuit, or from a supply cable damaged by work that seemed unrelated, such as a new fence post or a planting bed. Mention any work along the cable route, even if it happened months before the first trip.

Electrician or Gate Engineer

The two trades overlap, and the HSE describes gate work as often needing different skills, including electricians for wiring and checking the basic safety of electrical components. An electrician can isolate and test the supply circuit and its cable. A gate engineer knows the operator, control board and safety accessories, and how the system should behave once power is restored.

When you book, ask the gate company whether its engineer will test the electrical supply or whether you need a separate electrician. If two people are involved, share each one’s findings with the other. A gate engineer replacing a control board without anyone testing the cable, or an electrician condemning the motor without the gate being examined, leaves part of the question unanswered.

Part P, Notifiable Work and Certificates

In England, Part P of the Building Regulations covers electrical installations in gardens and on land associated with a home where the supply comes from the dwelling. Approved Document P gives a gate example: connecting an electric gate to an existing isolator switch is not notifiable, but installing a new circuit from the consumer unit to the isolator is. Replacement of a consumer unit is also notifiable, while repairs, replacements and maintenance are not.

Non-notifiable work still has to meet the safety requirements of Part P. For notifiable work, an installer registered with a competent person scheme can self-certify it. Approved Document P says such installers should complete a BS 7671 electrical installation certificate, with a Building Regulations compliance certificate given to the occupier within 30 days. Keep both with your gate documents.

BS 7671, the IET Wiring Regulations, is the national standard for electrical installations. The IET says BS 7671:2018+A4:2026 is now the current edition, and that the transition period for Amendment 2 ended on 15 October 2026. If a repair turns into new wiring or a new gate circuit, ask the electrician which edition they are working to and what certificate you will receive.

Details to Send When You Book

  1. Your postcode, the gate type and the make or model if you can read it safely from records or a label.
  2. The dates and times of each trip and what the gate was doing.
  3. Which device operated and whether other circuits lost power.
  4. Recent work near the gate or along the likely cable route, and any earlier repair reports.
  5. Whether the gate is your only vehicle access and how it has been left.

Questions for the Repair Quote

Ask what the engineer found, how the fault was confirmed and which component or cable section the proposed work addresses. Ask whether test results will be written down. If the trips have come back after earlier repairs, the decision about repairing gates that keep breaking down depends on that evidence, not on the number of visits.

There is no dependable fixed price for a tripping fault before the cause is known, because a damaged buried cable, a failed accessory and a wet control panel involve very different work. Ask for the attendance charge, the investigation scope and how any further work will be approved. If new wiring is needed, confirm who will certify it.

When requesting electric gate repair and maintenance, say that the gate trips the electrics and that the supply has been left off. That allows the right people to attend and the investigation to start from what you have already seen.

Tell us when the trips happen and what the gate was doing. Ask about investigating the fault and the repair work your gates may need.
